hero.titleLine1: How much more expensive is the basket?
hero.intro: Compare two national quarterly indices over the same period: one tracks prices paid by households, the other tracks wage prices for a comparable mix of jobs. Rebase each series to 100 at the starting quarter, then see where they go.
hero.noteBody: Index levels depend on their reference period. Here we compare percentage changes, not the raw index points.

learning.title: The two lines answer different questions
learning.cpiTitle: How much more do household purchases cost overall?
learning.cpiBody: The CPI summarises price changes for goods and services households commonly buy, weighted by their importance in household spending. The Australian national series is a weighted average of the eight capital cities. Every household has a different basket, so the CPI is not your personal bill.
learning.wpiTitle: How have wage prices changed for similar jobs?
learning.wpiBody: The WPI tracks wage price changes for a comparable mix of jobs, aiming to exclude changes in job content, quantity and quality. This chart uses the original index for total hourly rates of pay excluding bonuses. It does not describe any person's pay, hours, bonuses or after-tax income.
learning.normalizeTitle: Different reference periods: compare percentage changes
learning.normalizeBody: An index reference period is just the starting point for its scale. We set both selected starting quarters to 100; later values show each series' change from that point. The gap between the lines is the difference in cumulative index growth, not a difference in any person's purchasing power.
learning.normalizeLink: The comparable measures are trends and changes over the selected period.

world.realInitial: Nominal GDP per capita multiple ÷ CPI multiple.
world.realUpDetail: Nominal GDP per capita grew faster than CPI; the gap between the lines is {gap} percentage points.

world.calculationNote: Change after CPI inflation = (end ÷ start nominal GDP per capita) ÷ (end ÷ start CPI) − 1. Over long periods this differs a lot from the percentage-point gap: if prices double and nominal income triples, the gap is 100 points, but income after inflation is only 50% higher.
world.cpiBody: The World Bank republishes consumer price indices from the IMF's International Financial Statistics as annual averages, all set to 2010 = 100. Each country builds its own basket and method, so compare each country's changes rather than index points.
world.incomeTitle: Nominal GDP per capita (current local currency)
world.incomeBody: All final goods and services produced in a year, valued at that year's prices and divided by the population. Like CPI it is not adjusted for inflation, so the two can be compared; but it includes company profits and government revenue, so it is not household wages or disposable income.
world.noteTitle: What to keep in mind here
world.note.AUS: Above are the ABS quarterly CPI and WPI; this section uses World Bank annual data. Annual CPI is a yearly average, so it will not match any single ABS quarter exactly. GDP per capita is not a wage measure either, so it answers a different question from the WPI above.
world.note.USA: The selectable US years cover only years with both CPI and nominal GDP per capita. If one series is updated later, the range ends at their latest shared year.
world.note.KOR: Korean data begin in 1960. Over long spans both lines rise many times over and flatten the recent decades, so a shorter period is easier to read.
world.note.JPN: Japan's CPI was mostly flat or slightly falling from the late 1990s to the early 2010s, and nominal GDP per capita actually fell over that period. Try 1997 to 2012.
world.note.SGP: Singapore's GDP includes large profits earned locally by foreign-owned firms, so GDP per capita can sit well above what residents actually receive. Read it as output per person.
world.note.CHN: World Bank CPI for China starts in 1986, so China's years begin there. Figures cover mainland China.
world.note.DEU: Germany's money illustration uses euros. CPI and nominal GDP per capita each start at 100, so the chart shows growth. GDP per capita amounts in local currency cannot be compared directly between Germany and other economies.
world.note.GBR: The UK's money illustration uses pounds sterling. CPI tracks average consumer prices and GDP per capita tracks average output. Their changes help explain prices and the economy, but do not describe any individual's actual wage growth.

story.aria: Read the chart as everyday life
story.priceReading: Red ends at {price}: average consumer prices changed by {pricePct} from the start. A hypothetical {currency}100 spending amount indexed to CPI becomes about {currency}{price}. Your own mix of purchases can differ.
story.outputReading: Green ends at {income}: nominal GDP per person changed by {incomePct}. That average output amount can rise because more is produced or because selling prices rise. It does not mean your pay changed by {incomePct}.
story.wageReading: Green ends at {income}: wage prices for comparable jobs changed by {incomePct}. In a hypothetical job whose hourly pay follows WPI exactly, {currency}100 at the start becomes about {currency}{income}. This is an index illustration, not anyone’s actual pay.
story.outputAdjusted: Dividing the output-growth multiple by the consumer-price multiple gives a CPI-adjusted change of {adjusted}. It helps separate a bigger money amount from rising prices, but still cannot tell us each household’s income or living standard.
story.wageAdjusted: In that wage-and-price index illustration, wages relative to consumer prices change by {adjusted}. This divides the two growth multiples rather than subtracting their percentages. A real household also depends on hours, taxes and its spending mix.
story.cumulative: These are cumulative changes over the whole selected period, not annual inflation rates. Starting at 100 gives a common scale, not an actual price or income amount.
story.expand: Read on: everyday stories and historical turning points
story.historyTitle: What happened along this long path?
story.contextNote: These notes use official sources to highlight selected historical phases across the longer record; they do not disappear when you filter years above. Several forces usually operate together, and the curves alone cannot prove a single cause. Use the buttons to view the relevant period.
story.showPeriod: View this period on the chart ↗
story.flatLine: Remember: a flatter red line generally means slower price rises. Only a downward red line means average consumer prices actually fell over that part of the record. Lower inflation does not mean a return to old prices.
story.compareTitle: What can this table help me compare?
story.compareBody: Treat the vertical line as zero. Red bars show the cumulative change in consumer prices; green bars show the cumulative change in nominal output per person. Right means a rise, left means a fall, and farther from zero means a larger change. A longer green bar does not mean everyone earns more. The right-hand column divides the output-growth multiple by the price-growth multiple and subtracts one, separating bigger money amounts from growth after CPI inflation.
story.compareExample: If prices rise 100% and nominal GDP per person rises 200%, both are up, but the CPI-adjusted increase is only 50%. The table compares changes across economies, not where you could earn the most. Open each country tab for the historical stories behind the changes.
story.ABS.title: Why do payslips and shopping receipts move at different speeds?
story.ABS.intro: This quarterly chart is closer to a race between pay and everyday costs: red tracks average consumer prices, green wage prices for comparable jobs. Changing the starting point can change which leads. Following their changes helps explain why a pay rise may not feel like extra breathing room.
story.ABS.vignette: A fictional exercise: Zhou works the same hours and hourly pay rises from $25 to $27.50, or 10%. A comparable spending amount rises from $100 to $115, or 15%. Pay is higher, but it buys about 4.3% less: 1.10 ÷ 1.15 − 1 ≈ −4.3%. Simply subtracting the growth rates is not the purchasing-power calculation. Your own pay and spending mix can differ from the national indices.
story.ABS.takeaway: When red runs faster than green, average consumer prices put more pressure on comparable wages. The reverse creates room to catch up. Whether you can save more still depends on hours, taxes, rent or mortgage costs and what you buy most. Compare the same period, then check your own payslip and receipts.
story.ABS.event.0.title: The 2000 tax change: a step in the red line
story.ABS.event.0.body: GST was introduced in July 2000 alongside other tax changes, altering many final prices and producing a visible quarterly CPI jump. Policy can create a step in red without wages adjusting that day. This was not a 10% rise in every item, and the step cannot be projected as the annual rate forever.
story.ABS.event.0.source.0: Source · RBA · November 2000 Monetary Policy Statement
story.ABS.event.1.title: The mining boom: some jobs get larger pay rises first
story.ABS.event.1.body: Resource demand and mining investment increased the need to attract workers, with stronger pay pressures in mining and related industries. Green averages changes in comparable jobs nationally; it does not mean every industry got the same raise. Work opportunities in a mining region can feel quite different from service work elsewhere.
story.ABS.event.1.source.0: Source · RBA · Labour Supply During the Mining Boom
story.ABS.event.2.title: Slower wage growth: small price rises still add up
story.ABS.event.2.body: Wage growth weakened after mining investment cooled, against a background of labour-market spare capacity and cost restraint. A small raise can seem enough at first, but a gently rising red line eats into a budget if pay barely moves for years. Compare 2013–19 to see the lines gradually separate or draw closer.
story.ABS.event.2.source.0: Source · RBA · Low Wages Growth in Australia
story.ABS.event.3.title: Free childcare and cheaper petrol: an unusual dip
story.ABS.event.3.body: Temporary free childcare and cheaper petrol pulled CPI down in Q2 2020; some prices rebounded when free childcare ended. A dip in red did not suddenly make every household comfortable. Those without young children received less direct benefit, and someone losing a job could still struggle. Ask which items changed, then look at your bills.
story.ABS.event.3.source.0: Source · ABS · Consumer Price Index, June 2020
story.ABS.event.4.title: Prices move first; wages catch up later
story.ABS.event.4.body: Goods-supply bottlenecks and energy pressures after the pandemic lifted prices while wage adjustment initially lagged. Red grows faster than green over 2021–24, helping explain why some pay rises still felt inadequate. Contracts, labour-market conditions and policy affect when wages adjust. Lower inflation later slows further price rises without restoring the old shopping receipt.
story.AUS.title: Dearer coffee, a bigger economy: why can money still feel tight?
story.AUS.intro: The red line is closer to your everyday bills; the green line tracks the value of output per person across the economy. Two rising lines do not automatically mean everyone feels better off. The personal question is how your income, rent and usual purchases changed.
story.AUS.vignette: Imagine a fictional corner café. Raising a coffee from $4 to $5 increases sales revenue even if it sells the same number of cups. An employee whose pay stays flat may still struggle with a dearer lunch. The green line likewise combines output and price changes, and some gains may go to profits. It gives economic context, not the employee’s payslip.
story.AUS.takeaway: Treat the lines as a background map: red shows how far average consumer prices travelled; green shows how far the value of output per person travelled. Then check your own income growth and spending mix. A resources boom, higher café revenue and a pay rise for its staff are related, but different, outcomes.
story.AUS.event.0.title: High-inflation decades: pay and price tags both rise quickly
story.AUS.event.0.body: Australia did not always have modest inflation. Oil shocks in the 1970s combined with domestic wage, demand and expectation pressures, with inflation still elevated in the 1980s. Higher prices lift both nominal lines, so a large increase in the income amount is not all an improvement in living standards. A household’s pay rise can be caught by tomorrow’s bills.
story.AUS.event.0.source.0: Source · RBA · Inflation and Disinflation in Australia
story.AUS.event.1.title: Bringing inflation down has costs; stable prices are not cheap prices
story.AUS.event.1.body: Inflation fell sharply after the early-1990s recession. The inflation target adopted in 1993 helped lock in a lower-inflation environment. Red then rises more gently; it does not return to old prices. Budgeting becomes easier, but the transition also involved unemployment and business hardship. A gentler price line does not show how hard it was to find work.
story.AUS.event.1.source.0: Source · RBA · Twenty-five Years of Inflation Targeting
story.AUS.event.2.title: Higher resource prices lift the value of output
story.AUS.event.2.body: Demand from economies including China raised prices for Australian resource exports and encouraged mining investment. Green’s strong growth reflects production as well as export prices; not everyone received mining-sector wages. Recruitment, transport and services could benefit, while some households felt rising rents and costs first. The 2008 financial crisis also interrupted this period of growth.
story.AUS.event.3.title: After the boom, pay rises become a slower jog
story.AUS.event.3.body: After the mining-investment peak, spare capacity in the labour market and greater cost restraint contributed to slower wage growth. GDP per person is not wages, but this background helps explain why an expanding economy could coexist with disappointing pay rises. As long as red keeps rising, a household with nearly unchanged income can still feel squeezed.
story.AUS.event.3.source.0: Source · RBA · Insights into Low Wage Growth
story.AUS.event.4.title: From shutdown to reopening: supply struggles as demand returns
story.AUS.event.4.body: The pandemic disrupted production, transport and spending. Reopening brought demand back while supply chains, energy pressures and Australian floods constrained supply. Price rises steepen red and can also lift green, which is measured at current prices. Households face dearer food, fuel and services before pay necessarily catches up. Slower inflation later leaves those higher price levels on the bills.
story.AUS.event.4.source.0: Source · RBA · Supply and Demand Drivers of Inflation
story.USA.title: Pay is up, so why does the shopping cart still feel expensive?
story.USA.intro: A growing economy can mean busier shops and higher company profits without your pay keeping pace with the bills. Treat red as the background for consumer prices and green as the background for output per person. Then look back at your job and shopping cart.
story.USA.vignette: Fictional example: a US household buys a familiar mix of groceries, petrol and electricity each week. If that reference basket rises from 100 to 120, the same budget buys less of it. That does not tell us whether this family’s pay rose, or whether its own spending matches the CPI basket.
story.USA.takeaway: Think of a price shock as a basket of spending becoming more expensive, and the GDP line as average output across the whole economy. Even when GDP per person grows faster than CPI, not every household’s wages keep up. Housing debt, industry and employment shape what families experience. The chart offers a national backdrop; understanding a particular household still requires its budget and work situation.
story.USA.event.0.title: Growth continues as inflation begins to pick up
story.USA.event.0.body: Both lines rise through the early 1960s, while the CPI slope becomes steeper later in the decade. The Federal Reserve dates the turn toward higher US inflation to the mid-1960s and points to several demand and policy factors. Nominal GDP per person rises too, reflecting output as well as prices—not a general pay rise.
story.USA.event.0.source.0: Source · Federal Reserve History — The Great Inflation
story.USA.event.1.title: Oil shocks and the recession to bring inflation down
story.USA.event.1.body: After the 1973 oil-price shock, higher fuel and transport costs spread through many goods. Later oil shocks and elevated inflation expectations prolonged the price rise. Both chart lines climb sharply, yet GDP per person adjusted by CPI is roughly flat over 1973–82. Volcker’s tightening helped curb inflation and came with a recession; oil was not the only cause.
story.USA.event.1.source.0: Source · Federal Reserve History — The Great Inflation
story.USA.event.2.title: The financial crisis leaves a dip in the line
story.USA.event.2.body: Stress in housing credit and financial markets turned into a severe recession in 2007–09, with rising unemployment and falling output. In the annual data, nominal GDP per person dips in 2009 and the CPI slips briefly before both resume climbing. A national average cannot show who lost a job, carried mortgage debt or recovered first.
story.USA.event.2.source.0: Source · Federal Reserve History — The Great Recession and Its Aftermath
story.USA.event.3.title: Reopening demand meets supply bottlenecks
story.USA.event.3.body: The pandemic first disrupted production and spending. As the economy reopened, demand for goods recovered faster than supply, while chip, shipping and energy constraints added price pressure; Russia’s invasion of Ukraine pushed energy and food costs higher. CPI and nominal GDP per person then rose, after a brief GDP dip in 2020. Slower inflation does not undo earlier price rises.
story.USA.event.3.source.0: Source · Federal Reserve · Monetary Policy Report, March 2023
story.KOR.title: Fast-moving factories: will pay and bills keep pace?
story.KOR.intro: People in Korea feel price changes in groceries, transport, and housing. CPI summarizes prices across an average consumer basket. GDP per capita spreads a year of domestic production across the population and is affected by both output and current prices; it is not a personal wage or household income.
story.KOR.vignette: Hypothetical example: a parts maker in Busan gets more orders, adding value to GDP. Wages are only one part of the income generated and are shared across many workers. Higher GDP per person does not mean every paycheck rose by the same amount, and a nearby family's grocery bill may change at a different pace.
story.KOR.takeaway: Export orders, company profits, personal pay and shopping receipts are different parts of one economy. The two lines compare cumulative changes from a shared start. Knowing about crises and industrial change helps, but you still need your own pay and costs rather than putting average output straight into your pocket.
story.KOR.event.0.title: Export-led industrialization takes off
story.KOR.event.0.body: Both lines rise, with nominal GDP per capita expanding faster overall and CPI steepening in the 1970s as average consumer prices accumulated more quickly. That does not mean every item or household bill rose at the same rate.
story.KOR.event.0.source.0: Source · Korea Development Institute, Outward-Looking Industrialization Strategy: The Case of Korea
story.KOR.event.0.source.1: Source · IMF, The Years of Crisis (1979–80)
story.KOR.event.1.title: Stabilization and an export boom
story.KOR.event.1.body: After the 1979–80 shocks, policy shifted toward price stability, and CPI kept rising more slowly than in the prior phase. Growth picked up again from the mid-1980s as exports expanded, lifting nominal GDP per capita; CPI also accelerated for a time. The lines measure different things, and output growth alone does not show wage growth.
story.KOR.event.1.source.0: Source · Bank of Korea, economic history: 1980–1996 (Korean)
story.KOR.event.1.source.1: Source · Bank of Korea, stability-oriented policy and financial liberalization (Korean archive)
story.KOR.event.2.title: Recovery after the financial crisis
story.KOR.event.2.body: In 1997, capital outflows, a sharp won depreciation, and corporate and financial distress triggered a severe recession. CPI still rose in 1998, while nominal GDP per capita dipped only briefly before climbing again. Because the series uses current won rather than price-adjusted output, inflation can mask part of a real decline. Restructuring and export recovery supported longer-run growth, but gains were not necessarily shared evenly.
story.KOR.event.2.source.0: Source · IMF, 1999 Article IV consultation with Korea
story.KOR.event.3.title: Post-pandemic costs lift prices
story.KOR.event.3.body: Both lines nearly paused in 2020. GDP per capita then resumed rising, while CPI steepened in 2021–22. Disrupted supply chains and higher energy and commodity costs added pressure in Korea; they were not the only drivers. By 2024, the inflation forecast had eased, but the price index remained above its pre-pandemic level: slower inflation does not roll prices back.
story.KOR.event.3.source.0: Source · Bank of Korea, Inflation Effects of Individual Factors Causing Commodity Price Changes on Inflation (2022)
story.KOR.event.3.source.1: Source · Bank of Korea, Economic Outlook (May 2024)
story.JPN.title: Years of barely changing prices: is that always good news?
story.JPN.intro: Japanese households feel prices through food, commuting, and utility bills; CPI summarizes changes across an average consumer basket, not an exact reading of any one household bill. GDP per capita spreads a year of domestic production across the population and includes current prices, so it cannot tell us the wage or purchasing power of each person.
story.JPN.vignette: Hypothetical example: a family in Osaka buys rice, commutes, and pays utility bills, but its costs need not match the national CPI basket. If an exporter produces more value, GDP per person changes, yet that does not mean every worker got a raise. A surge in share or land prices also does not directly mean CPI rose.
story.JPN.takeaway: Share and land prices during the bubble were not everyday CPI. Long periods of low inflation also did not mean every household faced the same costs. Wages, rent, and household purchasing power require separate data.
story.JPN.event.0.title: Catch-up growth and oil shocks
story.JPN.event.0.body: Postwar catch-up expanded production and nominal output per person rapidly, while consumer prices rose steadily in the 1960s. Two oil shocks and domestic demand pressures made the CPI line much steeper in the 1970s. The index records accumulated prices, not the annual inflation rate; when inflation later falls, earlier price increases usually remain in the level.
story.JPN.event.0.source.0: Source · Bank of Japan, Price Developments in Japan: A Review Focusing on the 1990s
story.JPN.event.1.title: The bubble lifted assets, not just prices
story.JPN.event.1.body: Inflation slowed in the early 1980s. In the late 1980s, stock and land prices soared while CPI remained relatively stable. After the bubble burst around 1990, output and nominal GDP per capita lost momentum, while CPI continued to edge up. Separating asset prices from consumer prices explains why the bubble did not send the everyday-goods index soaring at the same pace.
story.JPN.event.1.source.0: Source · Bank of Japan, Price Developments in Japan: A Review Focusing on the 1990s
story.JPN.event.1.source.1: Source · Bank of Japan, Explaining Asset Bubbles in Japan
story.JPN.event.2.title: Low inflation flattens both lines
story.JPN.event.2.body: Bad loans, financial failures, and corporate balance-sheet repair after the bubble weighed on demand. CPI turned negative for a time in the late 1990s, and the global financial crisis brought another shock. In the chart, CPI ends slightly below its 1997 level, while GDP per capita in current yen flattens and falls. Even with zero inflation, prices can stay high; only a falling index means average prices declined.
story.JPN.event.2.source.0: Source · Bank of Japan, Japan's Economy and the Bank of Japan: Yesterday, Today, and Tomorrow
story.JPN.event.3.title: Import costs lift CPI again
story.JPN.event.3.body: Price changes were modest in the first half of the 2010s. Pandemic disruptions, a weaker yen, and higher global energy and food prices then raised import costs that gradually passed through to retail prices. CPI rose faster in 2022–24, while wages and service prices also began to matter. Even if annual inflation later slows, the accumulated index stays elevated. GDP per capita rising still does not mean wages rose in step.
story.JPN.event.3.source.0: Source · Bank of Japan, Japan's Economy and Monetary Policy (August 2024)
story.JPN.event.3.source.1: Source · Bank of Japan, Economic Activity, Prices, and Monetary Policy in Japan (June 2024)
story.SGP.title: A small island with high output: does everyone feel richer?
story.SGP.intro: Household bills in Singapore and production by multinational firms both matter to economic life, but they are not the same pocket. CPI describes average consumer-basket prices; GDP per capita averages domestic production at current prices, not resident wages or the income of a particular household.
story.SGP.vignette: Hypothetical example: a foreign-owned electronics plant in Jurong increases production, adding domestic value to GDP. Some profits may belong to non-resident shareholders or stay in the company; they do not automatically become a nearby family's wages. Average output for the country and one household's income can therefore follow different paths.
story.SGP.takeaway: Singapore's openness means exports, tourism, finance, and import costs can all bring swings. Keep domestic production, resident income, and consumer-basket prices distinct; GDP per capita is not the pay of every Singaporean.
story.SGP.event.0.title: From entrepôt trade to manufacturing
story.SGP.event.0.body: Around independence, Singapore used export-oriented industrialization and multinational investment to create jobs, while manufacturing and services expanded. Nominal GDP per capita kept rising. The 1973 oil shock slowed growth and made CPI rise faster. A small open economy feels both external demand and imported costs, so prices are not determined by local shops alone.
story.SGP.event.0.source.0: Source · Ministry of Trade and Industry, Singapore Economic Review Conference speech (2015)
story.SGP.event.1.title: Moving up after recession
story.SGP.event.1.body: The 1985 recession exposed weakening cost advantages. Singapore restructured, upgraded skills, and moved toward higher-value manufacturing and services. GDP per capita continued to rise quickly; CPI dipped briefly around 1986 before edging up. Output can grow without prices accelerating each year, and price stability has been central to Singapore's policy framework.
story.SGP.event.1.source.0: Source · Ministry of Trade and Industry, Singapore Economic Review Conference Dinner speech (2015)
story.SGP.event.1.source.1: Source · Ministry of Trade and Industry, speech on Singapore's innovation-driven growth (2024)
story.SGP.event.2.title: Long-run growth amid external shocks
story.SGP.event.2.body: During the Asian financial crisis, weaker regional trade, tourism, and electronics demand pulled GDP per capita down in 1998 and briefly lowered CPI; exports and services later supported recovery. The 2008–09 global recession brought a clear fall in nominal GDP per capita in 2008, followed by a near-flat 2009. The annual CPI index still edged up, just more slowly. Both lines rise over the full period, but the long-run trend does not erase short-run swings.
story.SGP.event.2.source.0: Source · IMF, Fundamentals and timely policy measures help Singapore weather the Asian crisis
story.SGP.event.2.source.1: Source · IMF, 2010 Article IV consultation with Singapore
story.SGP.event.3.title: Pandemic shock and imported inflation
story.SGP.event.3.body: The pandemic hit output and tourism services, followed by a rebound as activity reopened. GDP per capita first fell and then jumped; the measure also reflects its population denominator and current prices. CPI rose markedly in 2021–23, with imported costs, rents, transport, service fees, and the consumption tax all playing a part. Its pace eased in 2024, but the index stayed high. GDP measures domestic production; resident income requires a separate measure.
story.SGP.event.3.source.0: Source · IMF, 2021 Article IV consultation with Singapore
story.SGP.event.3.source.1: Source · Monetary Authority of Singapore, Recent Economic Developments (January 2024)
story.SGP.event.3.source.2: Source · Singapore Department of Statistics, National Accounts definitions
story.CHN.title: Factories produce more: does that mean more money at home?
story.CHN.intro: Families feel consumer prices when buying food and getting around; CPI tracks changes in the national average consumer basket. GDP per capita averages a year of national production across the population and is affected by prices and output. It is not a wage and does not show how gains are distributed. This China CPI series starts in 1986.
story.CHN.vignette: Hypothetical example: a small factory in Guangdong shifts from simple assembly to more complex products, adding value to national GDP. The gains are divided among wages, profits, and taxes, so households receive different amounts. Whether a family's food and transport costs rise depends on the CPI basket and its own spending.
story.CHN.takeaway: Price reform can make previously controlled goods reflect market supply and demand more quickly. When inflation later slows, the CPI index does not automatically fall. Rising nominal GDP per capita alone also cannot show that a typical household's income grew by the same amount.
story.CHN.event.0.title: Price reform and high inflation
story.CHN.event.0.body: Market-oriented reforms gradually loosened price controls. After further reforms were announced in 1988, a rush to buy goods and inflation expectations intensified; authorities paused parts of the reform and focused on stabilization. Reforms and demand expanded again in the early 1990s; CPI rose especially quickly around 1994, then inflation eased after tightening. Both the CPI index and nominal GDP per capita climbed rapidly, reflecting institutional change, production, and prices.
story.CHN.event.0.source.0: Source · World Bank, China: Reform and the Role of the Plan in the 1990s (1992)
story.CHN.event.0.source.1: Source · World Bank, China: The Achievement and Challenge of Price Reform (1993)
story.CHN.event.0.source.2: Source · IMF, China: Recent Economic Developments (1996)
story.CHN.event.1.title: Deflation first, then deeper trade links
story.CHN.event.1.body: In 1998, oversupply and weaker external demand during the Asian crisis coincided with falling consumer prices, and the CPI line dipped. Domestic-demand support followed as industry and exports expanded. WTO membership in 2001 deepened global trade links, alongside other reforms, infrastructure, and external demand; it was not the sole cause of growth. Nominal GDP per capita rose sharply, and CPI later resumed a gradual climb.
story.CHN.event.1.source.0: Source · National Bureau of Statistics of China, 1998 Statistical Communiqué
story.CHN.event.1.source.1: Source · World Trade Organization, China membership date
story.CHN.event.1.source.2: Source · World Bank, East Asia and Pacific Economic Update 2011, Volume 1: Securing the Present, Shaping the Future
story.CHN.event.2.title: Support sustains growth as prices fluctuate
story.CHN.event.2.body: After the global financial crisis hit exports, policy support cushioned the external downturn while investment and industry continued to expand. Nominal GDP per capita rose sharply. CPI also increased, but more gradually, with fluctuations tied partly to food and energy. Growth remained tilted toward investment and production, so average output gains did not mean household incomes rose at the same pace; rebalancing toward consumption became a policy challenge.
story.CHN.event.2.source.0: Source · IMF, 2010 Article IV consultation with China
story.CHN.event.2.source.1: Source · World Bank, East Asia and Pacific Economic Update 2011, Volume 1: Securing the Present, Shaping the Future
story.CHN.event.3.title: Output grows as CPI nearly flattens
story.CHN.event.3.body: After the pandemic, nominal GDP per capita continued to increase, while CPI edged up only slowly from 2020 to 2024. China official CPI rose just 0.2% in 2024, with categories such as food and transport moving in different directions. The property adjustment and subdued domestic demand added to low-inflation pressure. Low inflation does not mean costs broadly fell or that prices returned to an earlier level.
story.CHN.event.3.source.0: Source · National Bureau of Statistics of China, 2024 Statistical Communiqué
story.CHN.event.3.source.1: Source · IMF, 2024 Article IV consultation with China
story.DEU.title: From factories to family bills: when growth meets energy prices
story.DEU.intro: More cars produced, or higher export prices, can lift the value of output per person. A household may notice dearer heating and food first. Red and green help show why those changes sometimes travel together and sometimes part company.
story.DEU.vignette: Fictional example: a small café in Leipzig renews its electricity contract and orders coffee beans and bread. Higher energy or food costs can squeeze its budget, but staff pay, the owner’s profit and customers’ spending need not move together. National GDP per person is average output, not the money this café or its workers receive.
story.DEU.takeaway: Higher energy, material and food costs enter household bills and business budgets, and can then spread to other goods. Even when national output per person grows faster than CPI, not every industry or household shares the same gains. Keep the national average distinct from people’s everyday circumstances.
story.DEU.event.0.title: The post-war boom extends into the 1960s
story.DEU.event.0.body: The post-war economic miracle carried into the 1960s as productive capacity and average output expanded. In the chart, nominal GDP per person rises faster than CPI, though the reference basket also becomes more expensive. That gap is consistent with output growth, but it does not mean everyone’s pay, spending power or gains rose equally; the chart is a national average.
story.DEU.event.0.source.0: Source · Deutsche Bundesbank — Facing up to the original sin
story.DEU.event.1.title: Oil shocks and a relatively quick policy response
story.DEU.event.1.body: The 1973 and 1979 oil shocks raised energy, transport and production costs. German CPI accelerated, but the Bundesbank tightened policy relatively quickly and inflation did not reach double digits after the first shock. That does not mean the shock came without a cost. Both chart lines keep rising, and nominal GDP per person still mixes output with prices.
story.DEU.event.1.source.0: Source · Deutsche Bundesbank — Inflation: Lessons learnt from history
story.DEU.event.2.title: The national average changes after reunification
story.DEU.event.2.body: After reunification, the national average included regions with very different industries and productivity. The Bundesbank notes that East German firms entered the economic and monetary union with productivity well below western competitors. Nominal GDP per person then rose while CPI climbed more slowly; this reflects restructuring and changing output, not a pay rise for every household in either region.
story.DEU.event.2.source.0: Source · Deutsche Bundesbank — Germany’s economic union: incomplete convergence
story.DEU.event.3.title: Recovery meets an energy shock
story.DEU.event.3.body: The pandemic sharply disrupted production and spending in 2020. Reopening brought supply bottlenecks, and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 raised energy costs, adding to inflation and weighing on some output. CPI steepens in 2021–23, while nominal GDP per person first dips and then rebounds. Rising lines do not mean wages rose in step or every household became better off.
story.DEU.event.3.source.0: Source · Deutsche Bundesbank — War in Ukraine, supply bottlenecks and inflation
story.GBR.title: Bread, power and the pound: how do big events reach a bill?
story.GBR.intro: Fuel, heating and a loaf of bread bring energy prices, imports and economic conditions into a household budget. Growing output per person does not mean every paycheck rises together. Ask which changed first: your bills or your income?
story.GBR.vignette: Fictional example: a small UK bakery pays for flour, electricity and deliveries. When prices rise quickly, both the owner and customers may feel squeezed. Whether the bakery can raise prices, or staff receive higher pay, depends on contracts and market conditions—not on the national GDP-per-person figure.
story.GBR.takeaway: The same inflation wave affects households differently depending on how much they spend on commuting, heating and food. Average output per person also hides regional and industry differences. Even when nominal GDP per person recovers faster than prices, that does not mean every household’s wages have caught up with living costs.
story.GBR.event.0.title: Inflation rises after sterling’s devaluation
story.GBR.event.0.body: Prices were comparatively restrained in the early 1960s, then rose faster after sterling’s 1967 devaluation; the chart’s CPI is already climbing by 1973. A weaker pound can make imports and business inputs dearer, though exchange rates were not the whole story. Nominal GDP per person also rose, combining output growth with higher prices—not universal pay rises.
story.GBR.event.0.source.0: Source · Bank of England — UK Great Inflation, 1950s to early 1990s
story.GBR.event.1.title: Two oil shocks and repeated inflation surges
story.GBR.event.1.body: The 1973–74 and 1979 oil shocks raised energy costs. Sterling’s weakness and subsequent wage and price adjustments helped inflation return. The CPI slope is much steeper than earlier, while nominal GDP per person also rises quickly. Reading the latter alone would mistake price increases for an equal improvement in living standards; oil was not the only cause.
story.GBR.event.1.source.0: Source · Bank of England — Oil Shocks and the UK Economy
story.GBR.event.2.title: A slow recovery after the financial crash
story.GBR.event.2.body: The 2008 global financial crisis hit credit and investment, and UK output contracted from its peak before recovering slowly. In the annual data, nominal GDP per person falls in 2009 while CPI keeps rising. A household could face higher prices as its job and income prospects worsen. The average output line cannot show who lost work or recovered last.
story.GBR.event.2.source.0: Source · Office for National Statistics — GDP and events in history
story.GBR.event.3.title: Reopening, bottlenecks and energy bills
story.GBR.event.3.body: Lockdowns caused a sharp contraction in 2020. During reopening, a rebound in goods demand met supply-chain bottlenecks, while global shocks later pushed up energy and food costs. By 2024 the CPI remained higher overall, and nominal GDP per person had rebounded after falling in 2020. Lower inflation means prices are rising more slowly, not returning to pre-pandemic levels.
story.GBR.event.3.source.0: Source · Bank of England — Monetary Policy Report, May 2022
world.note.RUS: Ruble amounts are examples scaled by the consumer price index; GDP per person is still average output, not wages. Early Russian price changes were large, so a shorter historical window is easier to read. This chart cannot establish the ruble’s exchange rate or compare income levels across countries. In 1998, 1,000 old rubles were exchanged for one new ruble; these examples across years should not be read as the face values of old banknotes.
world.note.CAN: Money examples use Canadian dollars. Energy prices can affect both Canada’s resource income and household fuel bills; higher average output per person does not mean everyone’s pay has risen. CPI alone does not measure the price of buying a home.
story.RUS.title: More rubles on paper: why can life still feel tight?
story.RUS.intro: Pay, sales revenue and shop prices can all rise, but the practical question is how much those rubles still buy. Russia has experienced rapid price rises, resource booms and external shocks. Reading the lines together helps distinguish bigger money amounts before returning to household and small-business bills.
story.RUS.vignette: Imagine Nadia’s repair shop in Kazan. She still fixes ten items a day, but raises each repair price from ₽100 to ₽150, lifting sales revenue by 50%. If parts, rent and living costs also rise quickly, she may feel no better off. Higher parts costs can pass through to customers in repair bills. National nominal GDP per person likewise includes changing prices and output across industries; it cannot tell you what Nadia takes home.
story.RUS.takeaway: The key habit for reading Russia's chart is to separate rising nominal amounts from improving living standards. With high inflation, both CPI and ruble-valued GDP per capita can climb quickly even as real output, exchange rates and the distribution of income move differently. Slower inflation means prices rise more slowly; it does not mean prices broadly fall.
story.RUS.event.0.title: Market transition and the 1998 crisis
story.RUS.event.0.body: Price liberalization, disrupted trading links and institutional change brought a severe adjustment; CPI surges and ruble-valued GDP per capita expands rapidly. The 1998 crisis struck in the second half of the year. Here CPI is an annual average and GDP per person measures the year’s output. Both series nevertheless rise that year. That does not mean the crisis did not occur, nor that nominal increases represented more real output or better living standards. A household cares about how much bread payday money buys, not simply how many zeros were added to pay. The 1998 exchange of 1,000 old rubles for one new ruble changed the unit of account; it did not create purchasing power. The chart’s starting value of 100 is a reference for comparing changes.
story.RUS.event.0.source.0: IMF Working Paper: Russia's early price liberalization
story.RUS.event.1.title: Post-crisis recovery and energy income
story.RUS.event.1.body: Output recovered from 1999, and ruble-valued GDP per capita continued to rise rapidly; CPI rose too, but less steeply than during the early transition. Stronger energy-export earnings and improved terms of trade later provided important support. Import substitution after the ruble's depreciation and domestic demand also played roles, so the recovery cannot be reduced to one cause. Resource-sector orders and pay may benefit first; local shops and households can share the gains unevenly.
story.RUS.event.1.source.0: World Bank: Russia's commodity boom and growth
story.RUS.event.2.title: Global financial crisis and falling oil prices
story.RUS.event.2.body: The global financial crisis and falling energy prices hit export earnings, investment and demand. In 2009, nominal GDP per capita falls while CPI continues to rise: higher prices did not offset the decline in output value. The global shock reached Russia through trade, finance and energy markets, with effects varying across industries. A repair shop can face dearer everyday costs while customers delay repairs: rising prices and weaker business can coexist.
story.RUS.event.2.source.0: World Bank: Russia's economic diagnosis and the global crisis
story.RUS.event.3.title: Oil prices, sanctions and ruble depreciation
story.RUS.event.3.body: After 2014, lower oil prices weakened export prospects, while sanctions and financing limits added pressure. Ruble depreciation made imports costlier. The CPI line steepens around 2015, while ruble-valued GDP per capita still edges up but more slowly. Oil was an important backdrop, but exchange-rate and price changes had more than one cause. With dearer imported parts, a shop must weigh raising prices against accepting smaller margins; households may postpone imported purchases.
story.RUS.event.3.source.0: Bank of Russia: The ruble market in 2014
story.RUS.event.4.title: Pandemic, war-related shocks and domestic demand
story.RUS.event.4.body: In 2020, the pandemic and lower oil prices weighed on activity: nominal GDP per capita briefly fell while CPI continued upward. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, sanctions and changes to trade and payment channels disrupted the ruble and supply, and CPI inflation accelerated. Inflation slowed in 2023, then accelerated again in 2024, while the price level kept rising; nominal GDP per capita also climbed quickly. Demand, supply and sector mix all mattered, and the lines cannot show household gains or losses. For households, pay adjustments, product availability and different bills need not move together; average output amounts cannot capture these differences.
story.RUS.event.4.source.0: Bank of Russia: The pandemic's effect on activity in 2020
story.RUS.event.4.source.1: IMF: War-related sanctions and disruption to trade and payments
story.RUS.event.4.source.2: Bank of Russia: Demand, supply and inflation pressures in 2024
story.CAN.title: Oil prices fell, so why might life still feel expensive?
story.CAN.intro: Cheaper gasoline can help someone who drives to work. For a household with a job in the energy industry, falling oil prices may also mean fewer shifts or smaller bonuses. Canada’s lines put national consumer prices alongside average output, offering a backdrop without assigning every household the same gains or losses.
story.CAN.vignette: Imagine the Lins in Toronto. The same weekly basket goes from C$100 to C$110, while pay rises from C$1,000 to C$1,050. A 5% pay rise still trails that basket’s 10% price increase. This is a fictional exercise: national CPI need not match their spending, and the green GDP-per-person line is not their pay. Cheaper fuel may not offset dearer rent and groceries.
story.CAN.takeaway: Canada's turning points offer a useful distinction: a rising CPI index means the average price level is still accumulating; slower inflation means prices are rising less quickly. Nominal GDP per capita can fall during a recession or sector-specific shock even when consumer prices do not fall with it. Neither line is a full account of personal income or purchasing power.
story.CAN.event.0.title: Oil shocks and high inflation
story.CAN.event.0.body: The CPI line climbs faster in the later 1970s and early 1980s. International oil and food shocks raised transport, heating and production costs; wage and price expectations could reinforce each other. Nominal GDP per capita also rose, reflecting both economic expansion and higher prices—not simply richer households. For a household, a bigger paycheck still needs to be read alongside heating, fuel and grocery bills.
story.CAN.event.0.source.0: Bank of Canada: Lessons from high inflation
story.CAN.event.1.title: Making low inflation an explicit goal
story.CAN.event.1.body: After high and variable inflation in the 1970s and 1980s, the Bank of Canada and federal government set a path for lowering inflation in 1991. The CPI line is gentler afterward, while current-price GDP per capita trends upward overall. The target helped anchor expectations, but growth also depends on employment, productivity, trade and many other forces. Moderate inflation makes next year’s budget easier to plan; it does not restore prices from ten years ago.
story.CAN.event.1.source.0: Bank of Canada: The origins of inflation targeting
story.CAN.event.2.title: The global recession pulls nominal output per person down
story.CAN.event.2.body: The global financial crisis weakened US demand and Canadian exports, weighing on output, investment and employment. In 2009, nominal GDP per capita drops noticeably; CPI is nearly flat before continuing upward. A recession can therefore lower nominal output per person without requiring everyday consumer prices to fall at the same time. An export factory with fewer orders may cut shifts before a household sees broadly cheaper supermarket prices.
story.CAN.event.2.source.0: Statistics Canada: Key trade trends in 2009
story.CAN.event.3.title: Falling oil prices hit the energy economy
story.CAN.event.3.body: A sharp fall in world oil prices put pressure on energy-export income, investment and the Canadian dollar. GDP per capita dips slightly in 2015 while CPI continues to edge upward. That pattern is consistent with an oil shock, though two national lines cannot separate its effects from other sectors, exchange rates or policy. The same oil-price fall can save commuters money while squeezing jobs and local shops in oil-producing regions.
story.CAN.event.3.source.0: Bank of Canada Monetary Policy Report, January 2015
story.CAN.event.4.title: Pandemic shock, reopening and price pressures
story.CAN.event.4.body: Restrictions first weighed on activity and nominal GDP per capita. During reopening, recovering demand met supply bottlenecks, while international events also affected energy, food and transport costs. CPI rose faster in 2022; inflation later slowed, but the price level did not return to where it started. Nominal GDP per capita rose during the recovery. The forces did not contribute equally. If the Lins hear that inflation has fallen but groceries are still dear, distinguish the level of prices from the speed of their rise.
story.CAN.event.4.source.0: Bank of Canada: Post-pandemic demand, supply chains and prices
story.CAN.event.4.source.1: Statistics Canada: Consumer prices during the pandemic

china.calculationNote: Change after CPI = the income ratio between end and start, divided by the corresponding CPI ratio, minus 1. Because published index values are rounded, this result is approximate. It is a national average resident-income change, not any household's experience.
china.methodCpiBody: For 2013–2024, the National Bureau of Statistics fixed-base index is rebased to 2013 = 100. The 2025 value is linked using the published 0.0% annual-average CPI change. Published precision affects the calculation.
china.methodIncomeBody: Disposable income includes wages, business income, property income, transfers, and other sources. Wage income is one component and is averaged across all residents, including children and non-workers; it is not the average employee wage. Both measures are nominal yuan per person per year.
china.methodRealBody: Dividing the resident-income growth factor by the CPI growth factor estimates income change after consumer price changes over the selected period. A national average does not describe differences among regions, groups, or households.

Source pages and retrieval dates are listed below.

story.CHN_NBS.title: China: bring prices and income back to the household budget
story.CHN_NBS.intro: This chart compares average consumer prices with income per resident. Ask how much the same basket costs, then how much average income has grown. Resident income comes closer to a household budget than GDP per capita does, but it is still not your payslip.
story.CHN_NBS.vignette: Imagine a fictional household with two working adults and a child. Combined annual labour income is 120,000 yuan. Dividing by three residents gives 40,000 yuan per resident; dividing by the two workers gives average worker earnings of 60,000 yuan. These are different questions. Business, property and transfer income also enter the disposable-income account under its statistical definition. Do not divide the chart’s annual per-resident figure by twelve and call it a typical employee’s monthly pay. If this household’s income rises 10% while its unchanged basket costs 5% more, purchasing capacity rises by about 1.10 ÷ 1.05 − 1 = 4.8%. Its own spending mix can produce a different experience from national CPI.
story.CHN_NBS.takeaway: Bring three questions back to your own budget: did your income gain come from pay, a business or transfers? Did your usual purchases become more expensive than the national basket? After allowing for prices, can you buy more? The national curves provide context; your income sources and spending mix determine your own experience.
story.CHN_NBS.event.0.title: Starting in 2013: a shared household account
story.CHN_NBS.event.0.body: The unified urban/rural household survey began in 2013, standardising income names, categories and measurement. That is why this topic starts there; a definition change is not a sudden pay rise for everyone. From 2013 to 2016 the income line rises faster than the price line. A family might gain income by opening a shop or receiving a pension even if one member’s pay stays unchanged. Select wage income to focus on the labour-income component. It still averages across all residents and can reflect employment, hours and the mix of jobs, unlike the Australian WPI’s comparable-job wage-price measure.
story.CHN_NBS.event.0.source.0: NBS: unified household survey and income reform
story.CHN_NBS.event.1.title: 2017–2019: the market stall and the national basket
story.CHN_NBS.event.1.body: Annual CPI rose 2.9% in 2019. NBS linked the pork supply disruption to African swine fever and cyclical factors; annual pork prices rose 42.5%, with food a major driver of overall inflation. The figures are compatible: pork is one part of a weighted consumer basket. A household cooking pork frequently may feel more pressure than one buying little of it. Select 2018–2019 to compare one year of prices and income. The CPI change does not mean every item rose 2.9%. A supply shock can lift prices without explaining all movements in the income curve.
story.CHN_NBS.event.1.source.0: NBS: 2019 prices and the pork supply shock
story.CHN_NBS.event.2.title: 2020–2021: slower growth can still slope upward
story.CHN_NBS.event.2.body: The pandemic disrupted work, businesses and face-to-face spending. In 2020 average disposable income rose 4.7% in nominal terms and 2.1% after prices: it increased, but more slowly. A restaurant owner losing sales and a household with steady pay can coexist behind that average. Nominal income rose 9.1% in 2021. Recovery is measured against a disrupted 2020, so a rebound does not establish that every household recovered its losses. Select 2019–2021 to look across both years rather than treating the rebound year as the whole long-term story.
story.CHN_NBS.event.3.title: 2022–2023: reopening and uneven household recovery
story.CHN_NBS.event.3.body: Disposable income rose 5.0% nominally in 2022 and 2.9% after prices. As activity and service spending recovered in 2023, nominal income rose 6.3% while annual CPI rose only 0.2%, leaving less of the income gain offset by inflation. NBS also described this as recovery growth, with income foundations and consumer confidence needing reinforcement. A service-sector family receiving orders again may recover faster than another household. A rising average is not evidence of equal gains across industries, places or income groups. Use the ratio of income growth factors to price growth factors when calculating the adjusted change.
story.CHN_NBS.event.4.title: 2024–2025: flat CPI does not settle the household budget
story.CHN_NBS.event.4.body: Annual CPI rose 0.2% in 2024 and was unchanged in 2025, making the final price segment nearly flat. In 2025 disposable income averaged 43,377 yuan per resident and wage income 24,555 yuan, both annual amounts across all residents. Stable average prices leave less nominal income growth absorbed by inflation, but do not ensure better employment, business orders or personal pay. Cheaper groceries may not help a family enough if paid hours fall. CPI covers a consumer basket, not house purchase prices, loan principal or an entire household balance sheet. Unchanged annual CPI also allows differences across months and products; December’s year-on-year change must not replace the annual average.

wage.verdict.flat: Your pay roughly kept pace with inflation

wage.explainMore: {start} in {startPeriod} is worth about {required} in {endPeriod} prices. Your pay now is {gap} more than that.
wage.explainLess: {start} in {startPeriod} is worth about {required} in {endPeriod} prices. Your pay now is {gap} less than that.
wage.explainSame: {start} in {startPeriod} is worth about {required} in {endPeriod} prices — about the same as your pay now.
wage.formula: Change in purchasing power = (pay now ÷ pay then) ÷ (end CPI ÷ start CPI) − 1 = {wageRatio} ÷ {cpiRatio} − 1 = {real}.

wage.reference.wpi: For reference: the Wage Price Index (WPI) changed {value} over the same quarters. WPI tracks hourly pay rates (excluding bonuses) for a fixed set of jobs, so it leaves out job changes, promotions and hours worked. It is not average earnings, so it cannot tell you whether your pay grew faster or slower than the average.
wage.reference.disposableIncome: For reference: national per-capita disposable income of residents changed {value} in nominal terms over the same years. It is an average across all residents, including children and people not in work, not average employee pay.
wage.noteQuarterly: Australia uses ABS quarterly CPI (Table 17, original series A2325846C), precise to the quarter, covering {first} — {last}.
wage.noteAnnualNBS: China uses NBS annual CPI ({first}–{last}), precise to the year. Annual CPI is the average price level across the whole year, not the year-end level.
wage.noteAnnualWB: Uses World Bank annual CPI (FP.CPI.TOTL, {first}–{last}), precise to the year. Annual CPI is the average price level across the whole year, not the year-end level. No pay reference is shown: nominal GDP per capita is not pay.
wage.noteApprox: Source values are rounded, so results are approximate.
wage.notePersonal: CPI is a national average basket. Depending on your rent, commuting and spending mix, your personal inflation may be higher or lower.

scrolly.metadata.title: Scroll story: prices and wages in Australia | Everyday Economics
scrolly.metadata.description: Scroll through Australia's quarterly CPI and WPI since 1997: five historical phases, two lines starting at 100, and a calculator for your own pay.
scrolly.homeAria: Everyday Economics, back to the home page
scrolly.ABS.eyebrow: Scroll story · Australia · quarterly CPI and WPI
scrolly.hint: Scroll down to read. You can also press Tab to move from part to part, or ↑ ↓ while a part is focused. Each part states its key numbers in the text.
scrolly.numbers: {start} — {end}: consumer prices (CPI) {cpi}, wage prices (WPI) {wpi}; after CPI, wage prices changed {adjusted}.
scrolly.chartAria: Quarterly CPI and WPI index chart, both starting at 100. Current part: {title}. {numbers}
scrolly.ABS.intro.title: In {start}, both lines start at 100
scrolly.ABS.intro.body: Red is CPI, tracking household consumer prices; green is WPI, tracking wage prices for comparable jobs. The two indices have different base periods, so both are set to 100 in {start}; after that, height only shows the cumulative change from the start. Read on to see when the lines pull apart and when they draw closer.
scrolly.ABS.outro.title: What about your own pay?
scrolly.ABS.outro.body: From {start} to {end}, CPI changed {cpi} and WPI {wpi}. But WPI follows a fixed set of jobs, not any one person's pay: changing jobs, promotions and hours all give your pay its own path. Enter two of your pay figures in the calculator to check your purchasing power against the same CPI.
scrolly.error: The story data could not be loaded. Build the site first, then open it from the local preview address.
scrolly.sourcesTitle: Data and how to read it
scrolly.method: Both lines are rebased so the earliest quarter in the snapshot = 100. CPI is the ABS Table 17 national original quarterly index (A2325846C); WPI is the Table 1 private and public, excluding-bonuses original index (A2603609J). Each part's numbers are cumulative changes between its first and last quarters.
scrolly.contextNote: The historical notes follow the official sources linked in each part. Several forces usually operate together, and the curves alone cannot prove a single cause.
scrolly.entryTitle: Starting at 100: three decades of Australian prices and wages
scrolly.entryBody: Follow five historical phases as the two lines separate and converge, then check your own pay.

tm.reformNote.DEU: In {year}, German cash was the Deutsche Mark. €1 = DM 1.95583, irrevocably fixed from 1 January 1999; euro cash circulated from 2002. Amounts in marks are divided by 1.95583 to give euros, and results are shown in euros.
tm.reformNote.RUS: In {year}, Russia used the ruble from before the 1998 reform, which redenominated 1,000 old rubles as 1 new ruble. Amounts in old rubles are divided by 1,000, and results are shown in new rubles.
tm.reformNote.KOR: In {year}, South Korea's currency unit was the hwan. From 10 June 1962 it was replaced by the won at 10 hwan = 1 won. Amounts in hwan are divided by 10 and results are shown in won; all of 1962 is treated as won.

tm.story.deflation: From {early} to {late}, prices fell {cumulativeAbs} in total. That is deflation: cash left untouched actually buys {idleAbs} more.
tm.story.flat: From {early} to {late}, prices were essentially unchanged, and so was the purchasing power of idle cash.
tm.story.same: The two dates are the same, so the amount is unchanged. Move a slider to pick another date.
